title: SIMD & Vector Processing
summary: One instruction, many data elements at once. Learn how CPUs and GPUs exploit data parallelism for speed.

blocks.markdown:
**SIMD** (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) applies one instruction to several data elements at the same time, instead of one at a time.

- Adding 8 numbers normally takes 8 add instructions; SIMD does it in **one**.
- It's a form of **data parallelism** — the same operation repeated across data.
- Used everywhere: video, audio, graphics, ML, scientific code.
- CPUs have SIMD units; GPUs push the idea to thousands of lanes.

**Flynn's taxonomy** (1966) classifies machines by how many instruction and data streams they process at once.

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| SISD | One instruction, one data item — classic single-core |
| SIMD | One instruction, many data items |
| MISD | Many instructions, one data item — rare |
| MIMD | Many instructions, many data items — multicore |

Most real chips mix these: a multicore CPU (MIMD) where each core also has SIMD units.

**Data parallelism** — the same operation runs on many pieces of data (brighten every pixel in an image).

**Task parallelism** — different operations run at the same time (one core decodes video, another handles audio).

SIMD and GPUs target data parallelism. Multicore and threads target both, but shine at task parallelism.

SIMD needs somewhere to hold multiple values at once: a **vector register** — one register wide enough to pack several data elements side by side.

- A 256-bit register can hold eight 32-bit floats.
- One `add` on that register adds all eight pairs in one shot, lane by lane.
- Wider registers and more lanes generally mean more speedup, if the data is truly parallel.

A single SIMD `add` walks across every lane of two vector registers in parallel.

<<< Image: a clean horizontal diagram, blue/grey palette, generous whitespace. Two rows of 8 small boxes labelled 'Register A' and 'Register B', aligned above a row of 8 boxes labelled 'Result'. One big arrow labelled 'ADD (1 instruction)' pointing down into all 8 result boxes at once. 2-3 word labels only. >>>

Eight separate additions happen in the same cycle that one scalar add would take.

x86 CPUs added SIMD in stages, each widening the vector register:

- **SSE** (Streaming SIMD Extensions) — 128-bit registers, four 32-bit floats at a time.
- **AVX** (Advanced Vector Extensions) — 256-bit, then AVX-512 at 512-bit.
- ARM has its own equivalent, **NEON**.

Wider isn't automatically faster — code must actually keep those extra lanes full of useful work.

Two ways SIMD instructions end up in your binary:

- **Auto-vectorization** — the compiler spots a loop with independent, repeated operations and rewrites it with SIMD instructions for you.
- **Intrinsics** — special functions that map directly to one SIMD instruction; you write them by hand for full control when the compiler can't figure it out.

Auto-vectorization is easier and safer to start with; intrinsics are the fallback for hot, tricky loops.

GPUs take SIMD further with **SIMT** (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads): one instruction is broadcast to a large group of threads, each working on its own data element.

- It looks like normal per-thread code, but hardware runs the group in lockstep, SIMD-style underneath.
- A GPU has thousands of lightweight lanes versus a CPU's handful of wide SIMD units.
- This is why GPUs excel at graphics and ML — huge, uniform, data-parallel workloads.

blocks.sectionTitle: SISD vs SIMD vs MIMD vs SIMT
blocks.markdown:
How the styles differ in practice.

| Style | Best fit |
|---|---|
| SISD | Simple, branchy, sequential code |
| SIMD | One core, regular data, tight loops |
| MIMD | Independent tasks across cores |
| SIMT | Massive uniform work on a GPU |

SIMD and SIMT both exploit data parallelism; SIMT just does it with far more, simpler lanes.

SIMD/GPU speedups need work that is **regular** and **data-parallel**:

- Same operation, repeated over a large array, with little branching between elements.
- Examples: image filters, matrix math, physics simulation, neural network layers.
- Irregular work full of branches and dependencies (parsing, linked-list traversal) gains little — lanes sit idle or diverge.

Common mistakes:

- **"Wider registers always mean faster code."** No — if the loop has branches or dependencies between elements, the extra lanes go unused.
- **"The compiler will always vectorize my loop."** It won't if it can't prove the iterations are independent; you may need intrinsics or code changes.
- **"SIMT is just SIMD renamed."** It's SIMD-like execution hidden behind a per-thread programming model, at much larger scale.

blocks.subTitle: What is SIMD
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is SIMD and why does it help?**

SIMD applies one instruction to multiple data elements packed in a vector register, instead of issuing one instruction per element. It helps because it cuts the instruction count for regular, repeated work — more results per cycle without more cores.

blocks.subTitle: Flynn's taxonomy
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Explain Flynn's taxonomy in one line each.**

SISD: one instruction, one data item. SIMD: one instruction, many data items. MISD: many instructions, one data item (rare). MIMD: many instructions, many data items — how multicore CPUs run independent tasks.

blocks.subTitle: SIMD vs SIMT
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between SIMD and SIMT?**

SIMD is one instruction acting on lanes packed inside a single wide register, typical of a CPU. SIMT is one instruction broadcast to many independent threads, each with its own data, typical of a GPU. SIMT looks like normal threaded code but runs SIMD-style underneath.

blocks.subTitle: When SIMD/GPU helps
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When does SIMD or a GPU actually speed things up?**

When the work is regular and data-parallel — the same operation repeated over a large array with minimal branching, like image filters or matrix multiply. Branchy, dependency-heavy code gets little benefit because lanes idle or diverge.

blocks.subTitle: Data vs task parallelism
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Data parallelism vs task parallelism — what's the difference?**

Data parallelism runs the same operation across many data elements (SIMD, GPUs). Task parallelism runs different operations at the same time (multicore, threads). Real systems usually combine both.

blocks.subTitle: Auto-vectorization limits
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why doesn't the compiler always auto-vectorize a loop?**

It must prove the iterations are independent — no data touching the same memory in a way that changes results if reordered. Branches, function calls, or unclear pointer aliasing block that proof, so the compiler falls back to scalar code unless you rewrite the loop or use intrinsics.

blocks.subTitle: SSE vs AVX
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What's the practical difference between SSE and AVX?**

Both are x86 SIMD instruction sets; AVX just uses wider vector registers (256-bit, later 512-bit) than SSE's 128-bit, so each instruction packs more data elements per operation — more throughput for the same code shape.
